llm_response.content:
Below is a complete empirical plan for estimating the incidence of pregnancy-coverage mandates on wages, hours, and employment using the CPS and auxiliary data you described.

1. Identification Strategy
- Primary strategy: Difference-in-Differences with triple-differences (DDD)
  - For the state laws (May CPS 1974, 1975, 1977, 1978): Use a DDD that contrasts changes in outcomes for more-exposed versus less-exposed demographic groups in early-adopting states (IL, NJ, NY) before/after adoption relative to neighboring non-adopting states (OH, IN, CT, MA, NC) over the same period.
  - Rationale: The mandate changes the relative cost of employing a demographically identifiable subset (women of childbearing age and husbands on family plans). Leveraging within-state, across-group variation purges state-level shocks and general gender/age trends. Comparing to neighbors mitigates broader regional shocks.
- Complementary strategy: Event study (dynamic DID)
  - For the state laws: Estimate dynamic effects by event time to assess pre-trends and post-trends.
- Federal law (March CPS 1978, 1979, 1981, 1982; labor years 1977, 1978, 1980, 1981): Group-time DID
  - Since the PDA “treats” all states around the same time, identify using cross-group exposure differences nationally: compare more-exposed to less-exposed groups before vs after 1978.
- Intensity design (preferred within both settings): Replace binary exposure with a continuous, predicted cost-exposure measure built from the national insurer’s maternity add-on pricing (by age and coverage type) multiplied by the probability the worker is insured and on a given coverage type (imputed from the 1979 CPS Pension Supplement or NMES). This yields a plausibly exogenous treatment intensity.

2. Treatment and Control
- Unit: Individual wage-earner aged 20–65 (excluding self-employed; trim wages below $1/hour and above $100/hour in 1978 dollars).
- Outcomes:
  - Log hourly wage (employed sample)
  - Weekly hours (employed sample)
  - Employment indicator (any work in reference week or employment during year, depending on CPS file)
- Treatment timing/events:
  - State mandates: IL, NJ, NY take effect between Jul 1976–Jan 1977. With yearly CPS, code 1977+ as “post” for those states; 1974–1975 as “pre”. Neighbors (OH, IN, CT, MA, NC) serve as untreated comparators.
  - Federal PDA: Effective Oct 1978. In March CPS labor-years, treat 1980 and 1981 as “post”; 1977 and 1978 as “pre” (since March 1979 covers 1978 labor-market outcomes).
- Treatment variable(s):
  - Binary exposure (for transparency and baseline):
    - More-exposed group: women aged 20–40; married men aged 20–40 (as a proxy for husbands likely to be on family plans). Less-exposed group: women 45–55; unmarried men 20–40; men 45–55.
  - Continuous intensity exposure (preferred):
    - Construct E_i = p(insured_i) × [female_i × c_single(age_i) + married_male_i × c_family(age_i)], where c_single and c_family are the dollar annual costs from the insurer’s pricing for adding maternity coverage, mapped by age and coverage type; p(insured_i) and p(family|insured, i) imputed from the 1979 CPS Supplement or NMES for demographic cells defined by sex×age×education×marital status (and, if feasible, industry/union). This yields a dollar-cost exposure per worker.
  - State-law treatment indicator Mandate_st: 1 if worker is in IL/NJ/NY in 1977–78; 0 if in OH/IN/CT/MA/NC in those years or any state in 1974–75.
  - Federal Post_t: 1 for 1980–1981; 0 for 1977–1978.
- Control groups/counterfactual:
  - State-law DDD: Neighbor states (OH, IN, CT, MA, NC) over the same years; less-exposed demographic groups within all states.
  - Federal DID: National less-exposed groups over the same years.
- Event time:
  - For the event study in the state sample: define event time k = year − adoption_year_s, with adoption_year_s = 1977 for IL/NJ/NY (given annual data). Never-treated neighbors have no event.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- Parallel trends in absence of treatment:
  - For state laws (DDD): Absent the mandate, differences between more- and less-exposed groups would have evolved similarly in early-adopting states and neighbors. Plausible because we restrict to adjacent states, short window (1974–1978), and include rich controls.
  - For federal law (group-time DID): Absent the PDA, more- and less-exposed groups would have had similar national trends. Plausible if there were no contemporaneous group-specific shocks coinciding with 1978–1980.
- No policy anticipation that differentially affects treated groups pre-implementation:
  - The state laws’ timing (mid-1976/early-1977) and our pre years (1974–75) reduce scope for long anticipatory wage bargaining specific to pregnancy coverage.
- Stable composition within groups conditional on observables:
  - The mandate should not induce large, differential sorting into marriage, fertility, or covered employment within the short window. We will test composition changes and run robustness with imputed insurance probabilities fixed at baseline.
- SUTVA/no spillovers across groups or states that bias contrasts:
  - Some spillovers (e.g., firms smoothing wage scales) could attenuate estimates, but within-state cross-group DDD mitigates bias if spillovers are not group-specific.
- Correct treatment measurement:
  - Using predicted exposure from exogenous cost schedules plus baseline insurance probabilities reduces misclassification and endogeneity from individual insurance take-up decisions.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
- Differential macro/industry shocks in adopting states around 1976–1978
  - Mitigation: Restrict to early-adopters vs neighboring non-adopters; include state and year fixed effects; add controls for state unemployment rate, industry mix, union status; allow for region×year FE; estimate an event study to test for pre-trends; optionally add state-specific linear trends (with caution given only two pre years).
- Endogenous policy adoption correlated with women’s labor-market trajectories
  - Mitigation: Use DDD that subtracts out gender/age-specific national trends; show no pre-trends in outcomes for more- vs less-exposed groups; placebo checks on older women and unmarried men; sensitivity to excluding any one treated state.
- ERISA preemption/self-insurance and selective coverage changes
  - Mitigation: Emphasize intensity design where exposure draws on insured plans; examine heterogeneity by firm size/union/industry where self-insurance was more/less prevalent; reweight by baseline insurance probabilities from 1979 Supplement; show larger effects in sectors with lower self-insurance propensity.
- Composition/selection into employment affecting wage regressions
  - Mitigation: Report effects on employment and hours; check selection by comparing characteristics pre/post; implement bounding (e.g., Lee bounds) for wages if employment changes are sizable; replicate wage results on consistent subsamples (e.g., full-time, full-year).

5. R Code Outline
Notes:
- Replace file paths and variable names to match your CPS extracts.
- Weights: use CPS weights if available (e.g., weight).
- We use fixest for high-dimensional FE and event study.

# Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(readr)

#---------------------------
# 1) Load CPS May files (state-law analysis)
#---------------------------
files_may <- c("cps_may_1974.csv","cps_may_1975.csv","cps_may_1977.csv","cps_may_1978.csv")
dt_may <- rbindlist(lapply(files_may, fread), fill = TRUE)
# Assume variables: state, year, age, female (1/0), married (1/0), wage_hourly_1978usd, hours_week,
# employed (1/0), race_black (1/0), educ_years, union (1/0), industry, weight

# Clean sample
dt_may <- dt_may %>%
  mutate(
    age = as.numeric(age),
    female = as.integer(female),
    married = as.integer(married),
    wage = as.numeric(wage_hourly_1978usd),
    lnw = ifelse(employed==1 & wage>1 & wage<100, log(wage), NA_real_),
    hours = ifelse(employed==1, as.numeric(hours_week), NA_real_),
    employed = as.integer(employed),
    state = as.factor(state),
    year = as.integer(year),
    weight = ifelse(is.na(weight), 1, weight)
  ) %>%
  filter(age >= 20, age <= 65)

# Define treated and control states
treated_states <- c("IL","NJ","NY")
control_states <- c("OH","IN","CT","MA","NC")
dt_may <- dt_may %>% filter(state %in% c(treated_states, control_states),
                            year %in% c(1974,1975,1977,1978))

# Mandate indicator: first post year = 1977 for treated states
dt_may <- dt_may %>%
  mutate(
    post_state = ifelse(year >= 1977 & state %in% treated_states, 1L, 0L),
    mandate = post_state
  )

# Exposure: binary and intensity versions
dt_may <- dt_may %>%
  mutate(
    exposed_bin = as.integer((female==1 & age>=20 & age<=40) |
                               (female==0 & married==1 & age>=20 & age<=40))
  )

# Optional: load external cost schedule and insurance probabilities
# maternity_costs.csv expected columns: age_min, age_max, coverage_type (single,family), annual_cost_dollar
# ins_probs_1979.csv expected columns: sex, age_band, married, educ_bin, prob_insured, prob_family_if_insured
costs <- fread("maternity_costs.csv")
insprob <- fread("insurance_probs_1979.csv")

# Map age to age bands in both tables for merge
make_ageband <- function(a){
  if (a<=24) "20-24" else if (a<=29) "25-29" else if (a<=34) "30-34" else if (a<=40) "35-40" else if (a<=49) "41-49" else "50-65"
}

dt_may <- dt_may %>%
  mutate(age_band = sapply(age, make_ageband),
         sex = ifelse(female==1,"F","M"),
         educ_bin = case_when(
           educ_years < 12 ~ "<HS",
           educ_years == 12 ~ "HS",
           educ_years %in% 13:15 ~ "SomeCol",
           educ_years >= 16 ~ "BA+",
           TRUE ~ "UNK"
         ))

# Prepare cost by age band and coverage type
costs <- costs %>%
  mutate(age_band = case_when(
    age_min==20 & age_max==24 ~ "20-24",
    age_min==25 & age_max==29 ~ "25-29",
    age_min==30 & age_max==34 ~ "30-34",
    age_min==35 & age_max==40 ~ "35-40",
    age_min==41 & age_max==49 ~ "41-49",
    TRUE ~ "50-65"
  )) %>%
  group_by(age_band, coverage_type) %>%
  summarize(annual_cost = mean(annual_cost_dollar), .groups="drop")

# Merge insurance probabilities
dt_may <- dt_may %>%
  left_join(insprob, by = c("sex"="sex","age_band"="age_band","married"="married","educ_bin"="educ_bin")) %>%
  mutate(
    prob_insured = ifelse(is.na(prob_insured), 0.6, prob_insured), # fallback
    prob_fam_if_ins = ifelse(is.na(prob_family_if_insured), ifelse(married==1, 0.8, 0.2), prob_family_if_insured)
  )

# Merge costs
cost_single <- costs %>% filter(coverage_type=="single") %>% select(age_band, cost_single=annual_cost)
cost_family <- costs %>% filter(coverage_type=="family") %>% select(age_band, cost_family=annual_cost)

dt_may <- dt_may %>%
  left_join(cost_single, by="age_band") %>%
  left_join(cost_family, by="age_band") %>%
  mutate(
    # Construct predicted dollar exposure
    exposure_dollar = prob_insured * (
      ifelse(female==1, cost_single, 0) +
      ifelse(female==0 & married==1, cost_family, 0)
    ),
    treat_intensity = mandate * exposure_dollar
  )

# Controls
dt_may <- dt_may %>%
  mutate(
    age2 = age^2,
    race_black = ifelse(is.na(race_black), 0L, race_black),
    union = ifelse(is.na(union), 0L, union),
    industry = as.factor(industry)
  )

#---------------------------
# 2) Main DDD regressions (state laws)
#---------------------------

# Binary exposure DDD: y ~ mandate*exposed + FE_state + FE_year + X
m1_wage <- feols(lnw ~ mandate*exposed_bin + age + age2 + race_black + educ_years + union + i(industry) |
                   state + year,
                 data = dt_may, weights = ~weight, cluster = ~state)

m1_hours <- feols(hours ~ mandate*exposed_bin + age + age2 + race_black + educ_years + union + i(industry) |
                    state + year,
                  data = dt_may, weights = ~weight, cluster = ~state)

m1_empl <- feols(employed ~ mandate*exposed_bin + age + age2 + race_black + educ_years + union + i(industry) |
                   state + year,
                 data = dt_may, weights = ~weight, cluster = ~state, family = "binomial")

# Intensity DDD: y ~ treat_intensity + FE_state + FE_year + X
m2_wage <- feols(lnw ~ treat_intensity + age + age2 + race_black + educ_years + union + i(industry) |
                   state + year,
                 data = dt_may, weights = ~weight, cluster = ~state)

# Event study (Sun & Abraham) interacted with exposure
# Need adoption cohort for treated; 0 for never-treated neighbors
dt_may <- dt_may %>%
  mutate(adopt_year = ifelse(state %in% treated_states, 1977L, 0L))

es_wage <- feols(lnw ~ sunab(adopt_year, year):exposed_bin + age + age2 + race_black + educ_years + union + i(industry) |
                   state + year,
                 data = dt_may, weights = ~weight, cluster = ~state)

#---------------------------
# 3) Load CPS March files (federal PDA analysis)
#---------------------------
files_mar <- c("cps_march_1978.csv","cps_march_1979.csv","cps_march_1981.csv","cps_march_1982.csv")
dt_mar <- rbindlist(lapply(files_mar, fread), fill = TRUE)

# Assume it contains labor-year variable labor_year in {1977, 1978, 1980, 1981}
dt_mar <- dt_mar %>%
  mutate(
    state = as.factor(state),
    year = as.integer(labor_year),
    age = as.numeric(age),
    female = as.integer(female),
    married = as.integer(married),
    wage = as.numeric(wage_hourly_1978usd),
    lnw = ifelse(employed==1 & wage>1 & wage<100, log(wage), NA_real_),
    hours = ifelse(employed==1, as.numeric(hours_week), NA_real_),
    employed = as.integer(employed),
    weight = ifelse(is.na(weight), 1, weight)
  ) %>% filter(age>=20, age<=65, year %in% c(1977,1978,1980,1981))

# Build exposure the same way
dt_mar <- dt_mar %>%
  mutate(age_band = sapply(age, make_ageband),
         sex = ifelse(female==1,"F","M"),
         educ_bin = case_when(
           educ_years < 12 ~ "<HS",
           educ_years == 12 ~ "HS",
           educ_years %in% 13:15 ~ "SomeCol",
           educ_years >= 16 ~ "BA+",
           TRUE ~ "UNK"
         )) %>%
  left_join(insprob, by = c("sex","age_band","married","educ_bin")) %>%
  left_join(cost_single, by="age_band") %>%
  left_join(cost_family, by="age_band") %>%
  mutate(
    prob_insured = ifelse(is.na(prob_insured), 0.6, prob_insured),
    prob_fam_if_ins = ifelse(is.na(prob_family_if_insured), ifelse(married==1, 0.8, 0.2), prob_family_if_insured),
    exposure_dollar = prob_insured * (
      ifelse(female==1, cost_single, 0) +
      ifelse(female==0 & married==1, cost_family, 0)
    ),
    exposed_bin = as.integer((female==1 & age>=20 & age<=40) |
                               (female==0 & married==1 & age>=20 & age<=40)),
    post_pda = as.integer(year >= 1980)
  )

# Federal DID with group exposure
f1_wage_bin <- feols(lnw ~ post_pda*exposed_bin + age + age2 + race_black + educ_years + union + i(industry) |
                       state + year,
                     data = dt_mar, weights = ~weight, cluster = ~state)

f1_wage_int <- feols(lnw ~ post_pda*exposure_dollar + age + age2 + race_black + educ_years + union + i(industry) |
                       state + year,
                     data = dt_mar, weights = ~weight, cluster = ~state)

# Robustness: add region×year FE to absorb macro variation
dt_mar <- dt_mar %>% mutate(region = as.factor(region)) # supply this if available
f1_wage_int_r <- feols(lnw ~ post_pda*exposure_dollar + age + age2 + race_black + educ_years + union + i(industry) |
                         state + year + region^year,
                       data = dt_mar, weights = ~weight, cluster = ~state)

#---------------------------
# 4) One robustness check: placebo on less-exposed groups only
#---------------------------
# Placebo: estimate effect on older women (45–55) vs men 45–55 in state-law sample; expect ~0
dt_placebo <- dt_may %>%
  filter(age>=45, age<=55) %>%
  mutate(exposed_old = as.integer(female==1))
placebo_wage <- feols(lnw ~ mandate*exposed_old + age + age2 + race_black + educ_years + union + i(industry) |
                        state + year,
                      data = dt_placebo, weights = ~weight, cluster = ~state)

# Print summaries
etable(m1_wage, m2_wage, es_wage, f1_wage_bin, f1_wage_int, f1_wage_int_r, placebo_wage,
       se = "cluster")

6. Expected Results
- Wages:
  - Theory predicts partial to substantial incidence on wages for the groups whose expected benefit cost rises. Given annual maternity add-on costs equivalent to roughly 1–5% of weekly earnings for the most-exposed insured workers, I expect:
    - Women 20–40: wage declines of about 0.5–2% on average (diluted by uninsured workers and self-insurance exemptions), larger where insurance coverage is high.
    - Married men 20–40: smaller wage declines (e.g., 0.3–1%), reflecting family-plan incidence.
  - Using intensity (dollar exposure), coefficients should translate to roughly 0.6–1.0 cents lower hourly wage per $1 increase in annual expected maternity cost divided by typical work hours; equivalently, 30–80% pass-through of the mandate’s cost for insured workers, attenuated in the full sample.
- Hours and employment:
  - Small negative effects, likely near zero to modest: hours −0.2 to −0.5 per week; employment −0.1 to −0.4 percentage points. I do not expect large disemployment given the modest cost shares and the ability to adjust wages/benefits.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID/DDD)
- C1: Pre-trends/parallel trends supported by evidence (event-study, placebo) — 0.7
  - We can test with two pre years for states and two pre years for the federal analysis; limited but informative.
- C2: No anticipation — 0.8
  - Annual data and mid-1976/early-1977 enactments limit scope; we will check for pre-trend breaks.
- C3: No important concurrent confounders — 0.6
  - 1970s macro volatility and industry shocks are concerns; mitigated with neighbor controls, FE, and added macro controls.
- C4: Stable composition/no sorting — 0.6
  - Some selection into insured jobs is possible; intensity design using baseline probabilities reduces bias; we will check compositional shifts.
- C5: SUTVA/no spillovers/misclassification — 0.7
  - Some spillovers and self-insurance carve-outs may attenuate effects; using intensity and heterogeneity by sectors addresses this.

Notes on implementation and reporting
- Always weight by CPS weights and cluster at the state level for state-law analyses; for federal DID, cluster by state (and consider two-way clustering by state and demographic cell if cells are treatment units).
- Report both binary and intensity specifications; the latter is preferred for interpretation and for addressing partial coverage.
- Present:
  - DDD main tables for wages, hours, employment.
  - Event-study plots with pre-period coefficients.
  - Heterogeneity by union status, industry, and proxies for firm size (if available).
  - Placebo tests on older cohorts and on outcomes unlikely to respond.
- Translate coefficients into pass-through shares by relating wage effects to the predicted cost amounts, separately for insured subsets and the full population.
